rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to elute all 8 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window without risking truncation. This run should reveal whether peaks are compressed early, late, or across the full range so the next injection can trim the phi window and adjust slope.

All 8 compounds eluted by 9.4 min with only one critical pair, so keep the same composition window and temperature and make the gradient much shallower to test whether pair (4,5) is slope-sensitive. This directly tells us whether longer tG can resolve the pair or whether we need to change temperature or the phi window instead.

The critical pair is clearly slope-sensitive: tG 40 fully resolves everything but is too slow, while tG 20 is fast but fails at one pair. Interpolate to a moderate gradient length to target full resolution while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

The interpolation shows the critical pair improves with shallower slope but not enough at 24 min, so step to 28 min to approach the minimum tG that fully resolves all pairs. This is the most efficient next test before exploring temperature or window changes.

The critical pair is slope-sensitive but the broad window is wasting gradient range because all peaks elute in a narrow phi band, so test temperature next to shift selectivity without incurring a time penalty from a longer tG. Lowering T should increase retention and can change the close-pair ordering/selectivity enough to improve the unresolved pair while keeping all compounds observed.

At 25 C the separation is nearly ideal, with only one pair slightly below 1.5 and a small time penalty, so make the gradient just a bit shallower to push that pair over the threshold with minimal extra run time. This is the highest-probability route to a fully resolved method near the optimum.

We now know full resolution is possible, so the objective is to recover time while preserving the improved selectivity seen at low temperature. Raise T one step from 25 to 30 C at the faster 20 min gradient to see if the borderline pair stays at or above 1.5 while pulling t_last back toward 10 minutes.

The peaks in the best run eluted within a narrow effective solvent-strength band, so compress the programmed gradient to that window to spend the full 20 minutes where the analytes actually separate. This should increase resolving power for the borderline pair without the time penalty of a longer tG.

Injection 8 achieved full resolution, so the remaining objective is to reduce t_last toward 10 minutes while keeping all pairs above 1.5. Shortening tG by one step with the successful narrowed window is the most direct way to improve CRF and locate the time-optimal fully resolved method.

The current method is fully resolved with only a tiny time penalty, so shorten the gradient one more step to see if t_last can be brought to 10 minutes or below while maintaining all resolutions above 1.5. This is the natural next move to approach the CRF maximum.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the only useful follow-up is to probe whether an even faster fully resolved method also scores 1.000. Shortening tG by one more step tests the boundary; if resolution remains complete with t_last under 10 minutes, it is equally optimal and faster.

The 14 min method still has comfortable resolution, but pair (3,4) is now the limiting one, so shorten tG one more step to find the exact speed limit before it drops below 1.5. This is the most informative boundary test around the current optimum.

tG 14 is on the edge of full resolution, with pair (3,4) limiting, so slightly narrowing the upper end of the gradient should make the slope a bit shallower in the critical region without sacrificing the already short run. This tests whether we can retain full resolution with the same 1.000 CRF while using a tighter, more efficient window.

Narrowing phi1 to 0.55 restored comfortable resolution at tG 14, so now retest the faster 12 min gradient within this tighter window. If full resolution holds, it would give another 1.000 method at the shortest gradient tried so far in this refined window.

The tighter 0.25–0.55 window preserved full resolution at 12 min with the same limiting pair, so one more reduction in tG will identify whether this refined window allows an even faster fully resolved method. This directly probes the new speed boundary around the current optimum.

At 12 min the only failing pair is (3,4), so slightly narrowing the gradient further should make the slope shallower in their elution region and may preserve full resolution at this short runtime. This is a focused test of whether a tighter upper bound can keep the 12 min method on the 1.000 plateau.

The tighter 0.25–0.50 window restored strong margins at 12 min, so retest 10 min in this narrower window to see whether full resolution can be maintained at the shorter gradient. This is the clearest next boundary test around the fastest potential 1.000 method.

The 0.25–0.50 window still gives full resolution at 10 min, with the limiting pair just above threshold, so step down once more to locate the true minimum tG for a perfect score in this refined window. This is the most efficient way to define the fastest robust optimum.

Since 10 min is the current fastest fully resolved condition and 8 min fails only at pair (3,4), narrow the window one more step to further flatten the gradient in the critical region while keeping the short runtime. This tests whether the speed boundary can be pushed below 10 min with a tighter phi range.

The 0.25–0.45 window gives full resolution at 10 min but is slightly too retentive, so the key question is whether the tighter window can still hold resolution at 8 min. This directly tests whether we can beat the current fastest fully resolved runtime without crossing the 10-minute last-peak limit.

The refined 0.25–0.45 window still gives full resolution at 8 min with the limiting pair just above threshold, so test 6 min to locate the fastest possible fully resolved method. This is the most direct remaining boundary experiment around the optimum.

At 8 min with phi1 0.45 the method is still fully resolved but right on the edge, and 6 min fails only for pair (3,4), so narrow the window one final step to further flatten the gradient in the critical region. This is the best chance to preserve a perfect score at the shortest practical tG already shown to be viable.

The lower phi1 alone made the method too retentive, so raise phi0 by one step while keeping the same narrow window and short tG to shift the whole elution band earlier without steepening the gradient. This tests whether we can retain full resolution and reduce t_last below 10 minutes in the refined 8 min format.

The 8 min, 0.25–0.45, 25 C method already gives a perfect score, so with only two injections left the best remaining information is whether a small temperature increase can preserve full resolution while offering an alternative selectivity profile. This checks robustness of the shortest perfect method without sacrificing the established optimum.

Use the final injection to test whether the 8 min fully resolved method can tolerate a modest temperature increase in the slightly broader 0.25–0.50 window. This probes robustness around the optimum while staying close to the best-performing fast methods.
